bib.title: Omnilingual ASR: Open-Source Multilingual Speech Recognition for 1600+ Languages
authors: Omnilingual ASR team (core: Gil Keren, Artyom Kozhevnikov, Yen Meng, Christophe Ropers, Matthew Setzler, Skyler Wang; plus Ife Adebara, Michael Auli, Can Balioglu, Kevin Chan, Chierh Cheng, Joe Chuang, Caley Droof, Mark Duppenthaler, Paul-Ambroise Duquenne, Alexander Erben, Cynthia Gao, Gabriel Mejia Gonzalez, Kehan Lyu, Sagar Miglani, Vineel Pratap, Kaushik Ram Sadagopan, Safiyyah Saleem, Arina Turkatenko, Albert Ventayol-Boada, Zheng-Xin Yong; leadership: Yu-An Chung, Jean Maillard, Rashel Moritz, Alexandre Mourachko, Mary Williamson, Shireen Yates)

question: Can one ASR system cover 1,600+ languages, including long-tail languages with little data, and let communities add unseen languages from a few in-context examples?
hypothesis: Because the training corpus covers many languages, training an LLM-style decoder on N context speech-text pairs from one language should generalize to languages absent from training (Section 4.3).
contributions: SSL wav2vec 2.0 models at 300M, 1B, 3B and 7B covering 1600+ languages
Supervised CTC ASR models fine-tuned from the SSL checkpoints
A zero-shot LLM-based ASR model that transcribes unseen languages from a few examples at inference
A massively multilingual ASR dataset covering over 300 languages, average 10 hours of transcribed speech per language

method.summary: A wav2vec 2.0 encoder is scaled to 7B and pre-trained on 4.3M hours of unlabeled speech, then fine-tuned on a 1,690-language labeled corpus (AllASR) with either a linear CTC head or a 1.2B Transformer decoder (LLM-ASR). A zero-shot variant prepends N context speech-text pairs to the decoder prompt, trained on N+1 same-language pairs. Language/script ID conditioning and speech translation are added with small changes.
method.task: multilingual character-level speech recognition, zero-shot ASR by in-context examples, X-to-English speech translation

datasets.name: SSL pre-training corpus (unlabeled speech)
datasets.size: 3.84M hours across 1,239 languages plus 460K hours with no language ID (about 4.3M hours total)
datasets.source: public data, partner and commissioned data available when encoder training began, plus a large internal unlabeled collection
datasets.preprocessing: long recordings segmented into chunks of at most 30 s

datasets.name: AllASR (labeled)
datasets.split: training split; dev and test splits per corpus
datasets.source: open source datasets, LTPP/internal/licensed data, African Next Voices, Open Multilingual Speech Fund, Lanfrica/Naijavoices, Omnilingual ASR Corpus
datasets.preprocessing: text split with SAT sat-12l-sm into segments under 200 chars; forced alignment; audio segments kept within [2 s, 50 s] by split/merge; WER filtering on the Omnilingual corpus with source-specific thresholds 150 to 250 WER (Appendix B) using a 7B CTC model; character tokenizer of 9,812 symbols (characters seen fewer than 5 times removed); transcripts with >=15% unknown tokens dropped

datasets.name: Omnilingual ASR Corpus (commissioned)
datasets.source: commissioned spontaneous speech from survey-style prompts; target 10 hours from 10 speakers per language over about 350-400 languages; to be open-sourced
datasets.preprocessing: QA: every language human-reviewed at least in small scale, 279 languages in depth; language-code validation on 206 languages found misattributed codes in 20

datasets.name: MMS-Lab, FLEURS, MLS, Common Voice 22, Babel
datasets.size: MMS-Lab-1143, FLEURS-102, MLS-8, CV22-76 (as named in the tables)

datasets.name: CoVoST2 and FLEURS (S2TT)
datasets.source: X-Eng training data largely reused from SeamlessM4T, FLEURS excluded from training

models.name: OmniASR-W2V-0.3B/1B/3B/7B
models.architecture: wav2vec 2.0 (conv feature encoder, Transformer encoder, quantizer; contrastive loss with 100 distractors)

models.name: OmniASR CTC (300M, 1B, 3B, 7B)
models.params: encoder size plus one linear layer
models.architecture: SSL encoder with linear CTC head over characters

models.name: OmniASR LLM-ASR (300M, 1B, 3B, 7B encoder)
models.params: decoder 1.2B; Table 14 lists totals 2.2B, 4.3B, 7.7B for 1B, 3B, 7B encoders
models.architecture: wav2vec 2.0 encoder + 12-layer Transformer decoder, model dim 4096, 8 attention heads, next-token prediction
models.init_from: OmniASR-W2V encoder; decoder trained from scratch (stated for S2TT)

other.language_conditioning: language+script ID embedding, dropped with probability p; final models use 50%

models.name: Zero-shot LLM-ASR
models.architecture: LLM-ASR with N context speech-text pairs in the decoder prompt
models.init_from: 7B wav2vec 2.0 encoder (w2v2 seed); CTC-seeded variant generalised worse

training.objective: SSL: wav2vec 2.0 contrastive loss. ASR: CTC loss (CTC models) or next-token cross-entropy (LLM-ASR). Zero-shot: next-token cross-entropy on the target transcript after N context pairs.
training.optimizer: SSL: Adam. Fine-tuning: Adam with beta1=0.9, beta2=0.98
training.lr: SSL 1e-4; CTC fine-tune 1e-5; LLM-ASR 5e-5; per-language CTC fine-tune 1e-05
training.lr_schedule: SSL: warmup then polynomial decay to zero. Fine-tuning: tri-stage, warm-up first 10% of updates, constant next 40%, exponential decay final 50%
training.warmup: SSL 32K steps; fine-tuning first 10% of updates
training.batch_size: SSL (hours of audio per batch) 6, 5.7, 8.5, 17.6 for 300M, 1B, 3B, 7B; CTC effective batch 4.2 hours; LLM-ASR effective batch 2.1 hours
training.steps: SSL one million updates; CTC 200k steps; LLM-ASR 150k steps
training.regularisation: language upsampling p_l proportional to (n_l/N)^beta; SSL betaL=betaD=0.5; ASR final (beta_corpus, beta_language)=(0.5, 0.25); language ID dropped during training with probability p (50% in final)
training.hardware: Ablations: 1B CTC 100K steps on 32 GPUs; 7B LLM-ASR 150K steps on 64 GPUs; per-language CTC fine-tune about 1 hour wall time on 32 GPUs at 300M scale. GPU type and main-run hardware not stated.

other.pretraining_sampling: two-step: languages within each source from p_l=(n_l/N)^betaL, then sources the same way with betaD
other.per_language_finetune: w2v2 seed: lr 1e-05, 30K steps (converges around 10K); CTC seed: lr 1e-05, 5K steps; 11 low-resource languages with 5-10 h train and at least 1 h validation
other.s2tt: same hyperparameters as LLM-ASR; source and target LID tokens inserted; encoders W2V-1B/3B/7B

inference.decoding: LLM-ASR: beam search, beam size 5; CTC decoding not described
inference.samples: single evaluation per system; zero-shot context examples chosen randomly per utterance, same across models; no seeds or repeated runs stated
inference.prompting: zero-shot: <c> {<cs> g_s(x_i) <cs BOS> g_t(y_i) <cs EOS> </cs>} x N </c> g_s(x) <BOS> g_t(y) <EOS>; language-conditioned: g_s(x) g_t(<language>) g_l(l) g_t(<BOS>) g_t(y) g_t(<EOS>)
inference.retrieval: context examples by SONAR speech or text embedding nearest neighbours (sonar_ss, sonar_st), mean-pooled wav2vec 2.0 (w2v2), bm25 on target transcript (text_sim, oracle), top-5 character-bigram diversity (bigram), or the target pair itself (same_ex, oracle); similar examples ordered by increasing similarity

parameters.n_gram_LM_fusion: n-gram LMs trained on FLEURS and MLS training transcripts for the 7B variant; hyperparameters tuned on dev; values not stated

baselines: MMS (single- and multi-domain, with n-gram LM)
SeamlessM4T v1 medium/large, Whisper large-v2, AudioPaLM-2-8B-AST, XLSR-2B-S2T (S2TT)
non-zero-shot CTC and LLM-ASR trained with the same 32 languages held out
eval.protocol: Mean CER over languages per benchmark on dev and test; 95% CIs across languages for bucket and grouping tables; buckets high >50 h, mid 10-50 h, low <10 h of AllASR labeled data; languages with <30 min validation excluded; 14 language groupings; zero-shot: 32 held-out languages (half high-resource, half low-resource), CER pooled per language across eval sets. The authors caution against comparing numbers across heterogeneous benchmarks.

limits: Zero-shot performance does not match fully trained systems (Introduction).
Zero-shot models degrade on some seen-language datasets; separate models are released for seen languages.
Zero-shot study used 32 held-out languages, half of them high-resource; 14.4 CER on unseen languages is still high; context examples were random draws from the same dataset.
Low-resource bucket (<10 h) averages CER 18.0-18.6 and only 34-36% of those languages reach CER<10.
Dev and test sets are heterogeneous; the authors caution against comparing numbers across benchmarks.
USM comparison uses published numbers because USM is not public; no seeds or repeated runs, only 95% CIs across languages; GPU type, precision and total compute not stated.
text_sim and same_ex selection are oracles using the target transcript.
Ethics: compensation is not a panacea; capabilities may be repurposed for surveillance or unwanted moderation.
Language-code validation covered only 206 languages with 1-5 audio files each; 20 had misattributed codes.
